To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the history of North America soybean improvement is marked by two major events, namely the introduction of Asian soybeans and the subsequent hybridization between them and North American soybeans, and that the genetic structure of the soybean population is dominated by a single locus, maturity, and that the rate of change at the majority of loci is consistent with neutral expectations.
the genetic diversity of North American soybeans is comparable to available germplasm resources, and that the rate of allele frequency changes does not deviate from neutral expectation.

the structure and history (genomic and phenotypic) of North American soybeans are well described, and that the impact of recombination on the structure of the population and on the rate of allele frequency changes are clear, but the strength and nature of selection are less so.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the structure and history (including the impact of hybridization) of North American soybeans relate to the genomic signatures of selection.
how selection and recombination interact during adaptation to new environments and with how the resulting patterns are influenced by the history of the species.
the role of recombined diversity in the history of soybean improvement and how the genomic signatures of improvement can inform breeding strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic diversity of soybean has been severely impacted by breeding and hybridization, but that the impact of selection is more nuanced and difficult to discern.
selection has had a profound impact on the genetic structure of soybean, but that the impact has been uneven, and that recombination is a key component in the success of modern soybean breeding.
the impact of hybridization on the genetic diversity of soybean is not trivial, and that the impact of selection is not trivial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the impact of selection on the soybean genome is detectable, it is not so strong as to overwhelm the neutral forces of drift and recombination.
the history of soybean breeding in North America is characterized by a series of bottlenecks and selection, and the resulting population structure is highly clonal.
soybean breeding is a complex, dynamic process, but one that can be understood in the context of a few simple principles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the genetic architecture of soybean is not well described by simple models of selection.
, despite the long-term and extreme autogamy, soybean breeding has not been a purely clonal process.
the history of North America soybean breeding is a complex one, with many different forces acting in concert to shape the current genetic landscape of this crop.
